'''''Rhus glabra''''', the '''smooth sumac'''<ref>{{PLANTS|id=RHGL|taxon=Rhus glabra|accessdate=21 October 2015}}</ref> (also known as '''white sumac''', '''upland sumac''', or '''scarlet sumac'''),<ref>{{cite journal|title=American Sumac|journal=USDA Department Bulletin|date=1920|volume=706|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=X9hFAQAAIAAJ|access-date=30 April 2017|last1=Clerc|first1=Joseph Arthur Le|last2=Wessling|first2=Hannah L.}}</ref> is a North American species of [[sumac]] in the family [[Anacardiaceae]].

== Description ==
Smooth sumac has a spreading, open [[Habit (biology)|habit]], growing up to {{convert|3|m|frac=2}} tall.<ref name="tktimb">{{Cite book |last1=Turner |first1=Mark |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=VLbAAwAAQBAJ |title=Trees & Shrubs of the Pacific Northwest |last2=Kuhlmann |first2=Ellen |date=2014 |publisher=[[Timber Press]] |isbn=978-1-60469-263-1 |edition=1st |location=Portland, OR |page=370}}</ref> The [[Bark (botany)|bark]] is smooth and gray to brown.<ref name="tktimb" />

The [[leaves]] are alternate, {{Convert|30–50|cm}} long, compound with 11–31 [[phyllotaxis#Leaf arrangement|oppositely paired]] [[leaflet (botany)|leaflets]]. Each leaflet is {{cvt|5–13|cm|frac=4}} long, with a [[serrated]] margin.<ref name="tktimb" /> The leaves turn scarlet in the fall.

The species is [[dioecious]].<ref name="tktimb" /> The [[flower]]s are tiny, green, produced in dense erect [[panicle]]s {{convert|10–25|cm|abbr=on|frac=2}} tall, in the [[Spring (season)|spring]], later followed by large panicles of edible crimson [[berry (botany)|berries]] that remain throughout the [[winter]]. The buds are small, covered with brown hair and borne on fat, hairless twigs.

==Distribution and habitat==
It is native to North America, from southern [[Quebec]] west to southern [[British Columbia]] in Canada, and south to northern [[Florida]] and [[Arizona]] in the United States and [[Tamaulipas]] in northeastern Mexico.

It can be found in a wide variety of habitats, from streambanks to dry and montane slopes.<ref name="tktimb" />

==Ecology==
In late summer it sometimes forms galls on the underside of leaves, caused by the parasitic sumac leaf gall aphid, ''[[Melaphis rhois]]''. The galls are not harmful to the tree.

==Uses==
Native Americans ate the young sprouts as a salad.<ref>{{cite book|last=Little|first=Elbert L.|title=The Audubon Society Field Guide to North American Trees: Eastern Region|publisher=Knopf|location=New York|year=1980|isbn=0-394-50760-6|page=549}}</ref> The fruit is sour and contains a large seed, but can be chewed (to alleviate thirst) and made into a lemonade-like drink. Deer forage the twigs and fruit.<ref>{{cite book |last=Little |first=Elbert L. |title=The Audubon Society Field Guide to North American Trees: Western Region |year=1994 |orig-date=1980 |publisher=Knopf |isbn=0-394-50761-4 |edition=Chanticleer Press|page=519}}</ref>

In 2020, archaeologists unearthed a pipe at a dig in Central Washington state, showing chemical evidence that a Native American tribe had smoked ''R. glabra'' either alone or in a blend with tobacco, perhaps "for its medicinal qualities and to improve the flavor of smoke".<ref>[https://www.frontiersin.org/articles/10.3389/fmolb.2020.00133/full An Ancient Residue Metabolomics-Based Method to Distinguish Use of Closely Related Plant Species in Ancient Pipes]</ref>
